wstep: This card describes the NCHFP instructions for freezing grapefruit sections in 40 percent syrup and grapefruit juice with or without sugar, at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower; the instructions do not include blanching.

akapity: Select firm, tree-ripened fruit that is heavy for its size and free from soft spots.
Wash and peel the fruit, divide it into sections and remove all membranes and seeds.
For grapefruit with many seeds, cut the fruit in half, remove the seeds, and cut or scoop out the sections.
NCHFP uses US measures: a cup holds about 237 ml.
Pack the sections into containers and cover them with cold 40 percent syrup made with extra fruit juice or water.
For a 40 percent (heavy) syrup, NCHFP dissolves 2 3/4 cups of sugar in 4 cups of lukewarm water until the syrup is clear, which gives about 5 1/3 cups; chill the syrup before using it.

Use just enough cold syrup to cover the fruit, about 1/2 to 2/3 cup per pint; to keep the fruit under the syrup, put a crumpled piece of parchment paper on top and press the fruit down before closing.
Select the fruit as for sections.
Squeeze the juice with a squeezer that does not press oil from the rind.
Sweeten the juice with 2 tablespoons of sugar for each quart (about 0.95 l), or pack it without sugar.
Pour the juice into the containers immediately.
NCHFP advises packing the juice in glass jars, to avoid off-flavors.

JarAtlas rule (cautious): for juice use only wide-mouth glass jars made for both freezing and canning, never narrow-mouth jars, because ordinary glass jars break easily at freezer temperatures and expanding liquid can break a narrow jar at the neck.

Sections in syrup count as a liquid pack: in wide-mouth containers leave 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace for a pint (about 0.47 l) and 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) for a quart (about 0.95 l); in narrow-mouth containers other than glass jars leave 3/4 inch (about 1.9 cm) for a pint and 1 1/2 inches (about 3.8 cm) for a quart.
For juice in a wide-mouth jar, NCHFP gives 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace for a pint (about 0.47 l) and 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) for a quart (about 0.95 l).
Use packaging that resists moisture and vapour, is durable and leakproof and does not become brittle and crack in the cold.
Pack the food tightly, leaving as little air as possible, and press as much air as you can out of freezer bags before closing them.
Do not freeze fruits or vegetables in containers holding more than 1/2 gallon (about 1.9 l): food in larger containers freezes too slowly.
Ordinary glass jars break easily at freezer temperatures; if you use glass, choose wide-mouth jars made for both freezing and canning.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): this card does not use narrow-mouth glass jars, either for sections in syrup or for juice, because expanding liquid can break such a jar at the neck.
Close rigid containers with a tight lid and keep the sealing edge clean and dry.
Label each package with the name of the product, any added ingredients, the packaging date, the amount and the form of the food, such as whole or sliced.

JarAtlas rule (cautious; NCHFP gives no headspace for metric containers): treat a container larger than a pint (about 0.47 l) as a quart, and for these sections and this juice do not use containers larger than a quart (about 0.95 l; a 1 l container is already larger), even though the general limit above is 1/2 gallon, because NCHFP gives no headspace for them.
Freeze the food at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower.
For faster freezing, set the freezer to −10 °F (about −23 °C) or lower about 24 hours in advance.
Do not overload the freezer: add only as much unfrozen food as will freeze within 24 hours.
Keep the freezer at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower, because at higher temperatures food loses quality faster; keep a thermometer in the freezer and check it often.
At 0 °F (−18 °C) fruits and vegetables keep their quality for about 8 to 12 months; after that they should still be safe, only lower in quality.
For the best quality choose the shorter time and use the oldest packages first.
Serve frozen fruit while it still has a few ice crystals: it is then less mushy.
Thaw the fruit in its package in the refrigerator, under running water, or in the microwave oven if you thaw it just before use.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): thaw juice in glass jars only in the refrigerator.

A 1 pound (about 0.45 kg) package of fruit in syrup needs 6 to 8 hours in the refrigerator or 1/2 to 1 hour in cool running water; fruit packed in dry sugar thaws a little faster than fruit in syrup, and both thaw faster than fruit packed without sugar.
Thaw only as much as you need at one time; leftover thawed fruit keeps better if you cook it.
Never thaw food at room temperature or in warm water: its outer layer warms into the danger zone of 40–140 °F (about 4–60 °C), where bacteria multiply rapidly.

Thaw it in the refrigerator at 40 °F (about 4 °C) or below, in cold running water below 70 °F (about 21 °C), or in the microwave oven if you will cook or serve it straight away (juice in glass jars: refrigerator only, see above).
Thaw in cold water only in a leak-proof package or bag, only while the water stays below 70 °F (about 21 °C), and only if the food will thaw in under 2 hours.
Freezing does not kill all bacteria, yeasts and molds in food; it only stops them multiplying while the food is held at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower.
Food is safe while it stays frozen, but once it thaws and rises above 40 °F (about 4 °C), bacteria that were present before freezing can begin to multiply.
During a power cut keep the freezer door closed: according to the FDA, a full freezer keeps its temperature for about 48 hours, or 24 hours if it is half full.
When the power comes back, the FDA says that food which still contains ice crystals or is at 40 °F (about 4 °C) or below is safe to refreeze or cook; you cannot judge this by look or smell.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): throw away a package that has no ice crystals and is above 40 °F (about 4 °C), or that you cannot check.
The FDA also says to discard perishable food that has been at room temperature for 2 hours or more, or 1 hour if it is above 90 °F (about 32 °C) outdoors.
